items.title: Localisation of a module at a multiplicative subset
The module-fraction relation is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Check reflexivity and symmetry directly. For transitivity, combine two annihilating-denominator equations with one common multiplier from the multiplicative set.

items.title: Addition of localised module fractions is independent of representatives
items.strategy: Start from two valid representative changes and clear both denominator changes at once to show the common-denominator sum defines the same class.

items.title: The localised scalar action is independent of representatives
items.strategy: Treat the ring-fraction and module-fraction representative changes separately and then combine them to show ((a/u)(m/s) = am/(us)) is well defined.

items.title: Universal property of localisation for modules
items.strategy: Send m/s to s^{-1}f(m) in the target S^{-1}R-module, prove representative independence from the previous well-definedness lemmas, and force uniqueness by evaluating every class at m/1 and 1/s.

items.title: Localisation of modules is extension of scalars
items.strategy: Construct mutually inverse maps S^{-1}R tensor_R M <-> S^{-1}M by ((a/s) tensor m) mapsto am/s and m/s mapsto (1/s) tensor m, checking balance and the inverse identities explicitly.

items.title: Localisation commutes with quotient modules and arbitrary direct sums
items.strategy: Identify localisation with extension of scalars, then use the published quotient-tensor isomorphism and the direct-sum tensor isomorphism to transport both constructions through localisation.

items.title: A localised module fraction is zero exactly when one denominator kills its numerator
items.strategy: Unpack equality with 0/1 in the localisation relation and rewrite the witness equation as an annihilation statement on the numerator.

items.title: Injective module maps remain injective after localisation
items.strategy: If a localised element maps to zero, apply the zero-fraction criterion in the codomain and then use injectivity of the original map to push the annihilating denominator back to the source.

items.title: Surjective module maps remain surjective after localisation
items.strategy: Lift the numerator of each target fraction along the original surjection and keep the same denominator.

items.title: Localisation of modules is exact
items.strategy: Use the tensor description plus right exactness of tensor products for the cokernel side, and the injectivity-preservation lemma for the left exact side.

items.title: Localisation commutes with kernels images and cokernels
items.strategy: Apply exactness to the standard short exact sequences defining kernel, image, and cokernel.

items.title: Localisation commutes with finite intersections of submodules
items.strategy: Realise a finite intersection as the kernel of the diagonal map to a finite direct sum of quotients, then localise kernels, quotients, and direct sums.

items.title: There is a natural localisation map on Hom
items.strategy: Send a localised homomorphism class f/s to the induced map on localisations, prove the formula respects the localisation relation, and check S^{-1}R-linearity.

items.title: The localised Hom map is an isomorphism for finite free sources
items.strategy: Identify both sides with a finite direct sum of the localised target by evaluating at a chosen finite basis and localising coordinatewise.

items.title: A finite presentation reduces localised Hom to the finite free case
items.strategy: Apply Hom to a finite presentation, localise the resulting kernel diagram, and compare the two rows using exactness and the finite free case on the surrounding free modules.

items.title: Localisation of Hom for finite and finitely presented modules
items.strategy: Prove injectivity from a finite generating set of the source, then use the finite-presentation kernel reduction to obtain surjectivity and hence an isomorphism in the finitely presented case.

items.title: Local criteria for zero modules and for injective, surjective, and bijective maps
items.strategy: Detect a nonzero element by its annihilator and a maximal ideal containing that annihilator, then apply the kernel and cokernel identifications after localisation to translate module tests into map tests.

items.title: A sequence of modules is exact exactly when all prime localisations are exact
items.strategy: Localise the sequence to get necessity, then test the homology module for zero by the previous local criterion.

items.title: Support of a module
A prime lies in the support exactly when some element has annihilator inside it
items.strategy: Translate nonvanishing of m/1 in M_p into the failure of every denominator outside p to annihilate m, and rewrite that condition as Ann(m) subseteq p.

items.title: The support of a cyclic quotient is its vanishing set
items.strategy: Identify (R/I)_p with R_p/I_p and show this quotient is nonzero exactly when the extended ideal I_p is proper, equivalently when p contains I.

items.title: A finite module has the union of its generator-cyclic supports
items.strategy: Localise a finite generating surjection from a finite direct sum of cyclic modules and compare vanishing on both sides.

items.title: For a finite module, support is the set of primes containing the annihilator
items.strategy: Use the annihilator-membership lemma for one direction, and reduce the converse to finitely many cyclic generator quotients whose supports are explicit vanishing sets.

items.title: Support in a short exact sequence is the union of the outer supports
items.strategy: Localise the short exact sequence and read nonvanishing of the middle term directly from exactness of the localised sequence.

items.title: Support of an arbitrary direct sum is the union of the supports
items.strategy: Localise the direct sum termwise and use the zero-module local criterion to see that a direct sum localisation vanishes exactly when every summand localisation vanishes.

items.title: Support under localisation is restriction to primes disjoint from the denominator set
items.strategy: Use the prime-correspondence theorem and iterated localisation to identify the localisations of S^{-1}M with the original localisations of M at primes disjoint from S.

items.title: The Jacobson radical of a ring
An element lies in the Jacobson radical exactly when one minus any multiple is a unit
items.strategy: Intersect over maximal ideals for one direction, and for the converse put a nonunit into a maximal ideal and force the corresponding one-minus-multiple to be a nonunit too.

items.title: Determinant trick for Nakayama
items.strategy: Write chosen generators of M as I-linear combinations of themselves, form the matrix I-A, and apply the adjugate identity to show a determinant in 1+I annihilates M.

items.title: Nakayama's lemma
items.strategy: Apply the determinant trick to obtain an annihilator in 1+I and then use the Jacobson radical unit test to force that annihilator to be a unit.

items.title: Generators modulo an ideal in the Jacobson radical lift to generators
items.strategy: Let N be the submodule generated by the chosen lifts. The quotient M/N is killed modulo I, so Nakayama annihilates it.

items.title: Minimal generators over a local ring are exactly residue-field bases
items.strategy: Use Nakayama for the spanning direction, and if a lifted relation over the residue field is dependent then solve for one generator and remove it.

items.title: Support of a tensor product of finite modules is the intersection of the supports
items.strategy: Localise at a prime. If one factor localises to zero the tensor localises to zero; if both local factors are nonzero and finite over a local ring, pass to the residue field and use Nakayama plus nonzero finite-dimensional tensor products over a field.

items.title: A finite module that vanishes at a prime vanishes on some principal neighbourhood of that prime
items.strategy: Use the support-annihilator theorem to find an annihilating element outside the prime, then invert it so that the localised module is killed by a unit.

title: Localisation of Modules and Support — Examples

items.title: Localising cyclic abelian groups and Q/Z at a prime
items.strategy: Compute Z_(p) tensor_Z Z/n from the quotient-tensor formula by separating the p-primary and prime-to-p parts, then show Q/Z localises to its p-primary summand.

items.title: Localising Z/12Z kills exactly the torsion seen by the denominator set
items.strategy: Work with the multiplicative sets generated by 2 and by 3, compute when a denominator power annihilates each residue class, and read the surviving fractions from the zero criterion.

items.title: The support of Z/12Z is the pair of primes (2) and (3)
items.strategy: Apply the cyclic-support lemma to the quotient Z/(12), then identify the prime ideals of Z containing 12.

items.title: The support of the direct sum over all primes of Z/pZ is the set of all nonzero prime ideals of Z
items.strategy: Localise each summand at a prime q and observe that only the q-summand survives, then apply the direct-sum support theorem.

items.title: Over Z, the ideal (2) acts surjectively on Z/3Z but does not kill it
items.strategy: Show 2 acts as an automorphism of Z/3Z, so (2)M = M, and then note that (2) is not contained in the Jacobson radical of Z.

items.title: The p-primary quotient Q/Z_(p) over Z_(p) shows finite generation is essential in Nakayama
items.strategy: Identify $mathbb Z_{(p)}$ inside $mathbb Q$ via the localisation definition and the field-of-fractions embedding, then show multiplication by $p$ on $mathbb Q/mathbb Z_{(p)}$ is surjective while the module remains nonzero and not finitely generated.

items.title: The ideal (x,y) in k[x,y]_(x,y) has two minimal generators
items.strategy: Pass to the residue field of the local ring k[x,y]_(x,y), compute the classes of x and y in m/m^2, and apply the residue-basis criterion.

items.title: The Chinese-remainder map Z/6Z -> Z/2Z direct-sum Z/3Z is an isomorphism by local tests
items.strategy: Check that localising at primes other than 2 and 3 kills both sides, and that at 2 and 3 the map becomes the obvious identity on the surviving summand.

items.title: Localised Hom can fail without finite presentation of the source
items.strategy: Use Altman-Kleiman's standard non-finitely-presented source module to show the natural localisation-of-Hom map is injective but not surjective, and isolate exactly where the finite-presentation kernel step breaks.

items.title: Localisation need not commute with infinite products
items.strategy: Follow Altman-Kleiman's infinite-product witness and compare the product of the localised factors with the localisation of the product by testing which families admit one common denominator.
